===== FILE: assets/README.md =====
# CleanFlow of Ohio — asset manifest

Every image the site renders is listed here with its ownership or licensing
basis. If an asset is not in this file, it should not be on the site.

## Principle

The site renders **no externally hosted imagery**. Every visual asset is either
tracked in this directory or drawn with CSS. That removes three classes of risk
at once: another party's server disappearing or blocking hotlinks, an unclear
copyright position, and photographs of unknown provenance being read as
CleanFlow's own work.

Where an authentic CleanFlow photograph is not available, the site uses a
branded media panel (`.brand-media` in `style.css`) rather than a stand-in
photograph. These panels are honest by construction: they present a service
name and icon, and never imply a job result.

## Tracked assets

| Path | Type | Size | Ownership / licence | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `assets/brand/cleanflow-mascot.png` | PNG, 820x365, RGBA | ~275 KB | **Owner-approved CleanFlow of Ohio artwork**, supplied by the owner. This is the company's official mascot and logo lockup. Cropped to its content box and downscaled from the 1536x1024 original; artwork itself is unaltered. | `/services/gutter-installation` hero; the social preview |
| `assets/og-image.png` | PNG, 1200x630 | ~454 KB | Layout and typography are original work for CleanFlow of Ohio; the brand mark within it is the owner's mascot lockup above. Rendered from `assets/brand/og-image.source.html`. Typeface: Liberation Sans (SIL Open Font License 1.1). | `og:image` and `twitter:image` on all six public pages |
| `assets/brand/hero-pattern.svg` | SVG, 1200x600 | ~2.0 KB | Original **decorative background texture** created for this site — abstract roofline, gutter run, and droplet motif. It is a pattern, not a brand mark, and is not used as a logo anywhere. | `#hero` and `.services-hero-wow` backgrounds in `style.css`; `/services/dryer-vent-cleaning` hero |
| `assets/brand/og-image.source.html` | HTML | ~4.5 KB | Build source for the social preview. Marked `noindex, nofollow`; not linked from the site. | Regenerating `og-image.png` |

## Brand mark policy

The only mark that represents CleanFlow of Ohio on this site is
`assets/brand/cleanflow-mascot.png`, which is the owner's own artwork.

No substitute, stand-in, or newly drawn logo may be introduced as the company's
mark. An earlier revision of this site briefly shipped an invented
droplet-and-channel emblem while the authentic file was unavailable; it has been
removed. If the mascot file is ever missing, use a plain CleanFlow of Ohio
text-and-pattern treatment and flag that the authentic artwork is needed —
do not draw a replacement mark.

`hero-pattern.svg` is a decorative background texture, not a mark, and is never
used in a logo position.

## Regenerating the social preview

`assets/og-image.png` is rendered from its HTML source with headless Chromium,
captured through the DevTools Protocol so the output is exactly 1200x630
(`--window-size` alone under-reports the layout viewport and leaves a white
band at the bottom).

Edit `assets/brand/og-image.source.html`, then re-render and confirm the header
reports `1200x630`. The source references `cleanflow-mascot.png` from the same
directory, so the preview always carries the owner's real mark.

## Contrast

Branded media panels place their label and icon on a `rgba(13, 27, 54, 0.58)` /
`0.42` scrim so contrast holds on every panel tint, including the orange dryer
and installation gradients. Measured worst cases: **7.32:1** for label text
(WCAG AA needs 4.5:1) and **5.07:1** for the icon glyph (WCAG 1.4.11 needs
3:1). Without the scrim, white-on-orange measured 2.19:1 and failed.

## Fonts and icons

| Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- |
| Poppins (Google Fonts CDN) | SIL Open Font License 1.1 |
| Font Awesome Free 6.4.0 (jsDelivr) | Icons CC BY 4.0, CSS/JS MIT. Free tier only — no Pro glyphs are referenced. |
| Liberation Sans | SIL Open Font License 1.1. Used only inside the social-preview render; the glyphs are baked into the PNG. |

These are typography and icon dependencies, not imagery. See the runtime
dependency table in the root `README.md`.

## Removed imagery and why

Everything below was previously hotlinked from a third-party server. None of it
was CleanFlow's, and none of it is republished here.

| Former source | Where it appeared | Problem | Replacement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nedstevens.com` | `#hero` and `.services-hero-wow` backgrounds; "Our Work" gallery | **Direct competitor's photograph**, including one of their staff presented as CleanFlow's work | `hero-pattern.svg` over a brand gradient; gallery rebuilt as proof-of-work cards |
| `cdn.prod.website-files.com` | Home service card, services detail, gutter-cleaning detail | Unidentified contractor's before/after, read as CleanFlow's result | `.brand-media` panels |
| `dlczb9lfz9r73.cloudfront.net` | Repairs and guards cards and details | Unidentified host; one filename indicates a **paid iStock licence held by someone else** | `.brand-media` panels |
| `images.squarespace-cdn.com` | "Our Work" gallery | Unidentified contractor's before/after presented as CleanFlow's result | Proof-of-work cards |
| `static.wixstatic.com` | "Our Work" gallery | Unidentified contractor's photograph | Proof-of-work cards |
| `i.ibb.co` | Installation hero mascot, installation before/after, installation `og:image` | Free anonymous image host with no retention guarantee; the before/after was unverified | Mascot now tracked locally as `cleanflow-mascot.png` (owner-supplied); before/after replaced with process cards; `og-image.png` |
| `images.pexels.com` | Installation card, dryer-vent detail, gutter-brightening detail | Licence was fine (Pexels licence), but each sat where it read as a CleanFlow result, and each was an external runtime dependency | `.brand-media` panels |
| `images.unsplash.com` | Dryer-vent hero background | Licence was fine (Unsplash licence); removed only to eliminate the last external image dependency. It sat behind an 85% overlay and was barely visible. | `hero-pattern.svg` over a brand gradient |

Pexels and Unsplash imagery was eligible to be retained. It was removed so the
"no external image hosts" guarantee is absolute rather than nearly true, and so
the visual system stays consistent now that the other panels are branded.

## Adding real CleanFlow photographs later

The branded panels are drop-in replaceable. To use a genuine job photograph:

1. Add the file under `assets/work/` (create the directory) at roughly 1200px
   wide, and record it in the table above with the property and date.
2. Replace the `.brand-media` element with an `<img>` carrying `loading="lazy"`,
   `decoding="async"`, explicit `width`/`height`, and alt text that describes
   what is actually shown.
3. Only describe a photograph as CleanFlow's work if it is.

Sections that would benefit most, in priority order:

1. **Proof-of-work cards on `/services`** — a real before/after pair from one
   job would do more for conversion than any other single image on the site.
2. **Gutter-cleaning detail panel on `/services/gutter-cleaning`** — the
   highest-intent page; a real downspout flow test in progress would be ideal.
3. **Installation section on `/services/gutter-installation`** — on-site
   roll-forming is visually distinctive and hard to fake.
4. **Home page service cards** — four real service shots would lift the whole
   page.
5. **Gutter brightening** — a genuine before/after is the only honest way to
   sell this, since the result is entirely visual.

  * { margin:0; padding:0; box-sizing:border-box; }
  html, body { width:1200px; height:630px; overflow:hidden; }

      radial-gradient(circle at 16% 14%, rgba(243,156,18,0.26), transparent 30%),

      linear-gradient(135deg, #1e3c72 0%, #24487f 45%, #2c5aa0 100%);
  }
  .ring { position:absolute; border-radius:50%; }
  .ring-a { width:520px; height:520px; border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.16); top:-210px; right:-140px; }
  .ring-b { width:300px; height:300px; background:rgba(243,156,18,0.13); bottom:-160px; left:-95px; }
  .ring-c { width:170px; height:170px; border:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.10); bottom:70px; right:130px; }
  .accent-bar { position:absolute; top:0; left:0; width:100%; height:8px;
    background:linear-gradient(90deg,#f39c12 0%,#e67e22 32%,#3a6fc7 68%,#1e3c72 100%); }
  .wrap { position:relative; z-index:2; height:100%; padding:52px 74px 54px;
    display:flex; flex-direction:column; justify-content:space-between; }
  .lockup { width:600px; height:auto; display:block; }
  h1 { font-size:47px; line-height:1.18; font-weight:700; max-width:1010px; letter-spacing:-0.4px; }
  h1 em { font-style:normal; color:#f6b545; }
  .chips { display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:10px; margin-top:22px; }
  .chip { font-size:18px; font-weight:600; padding:8px 18px; border-radius:999px;

  .foot { display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between;
    border-top:1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.2); padding-top:20px; }
  .place { font-size:22px; font-weight:600; color:rgba(255,255,255,0.92); }
  .phone { font-size:30px; font-weight:700; color:#f6b545; letter-spacing:0.4px; }
</style>
</head>

            <div class="container">
                <div data-aos="fade-up">
                    <h1 style="color: white; font-size: 2.8rem;">Dryer Vent Cleaning in Dayton & Surrounding Areas</h1>
                    <p style="font-size: 1.2rem; max-width: 760px; margin: 0 auto 30px;">Protect your home from fire hazards, improve dryer efficiency, and help restore proper airflow with professional dryer vent cleaning from CleanFlow of Ohio.</p>

                    <div style="background: var(--accent); display: inline-block; padding: 20px 40px; border-radius: 10px; margin-bottom: 30px;">
                        <div style="font-size: 1rem; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1px;">Summer Special</div>
                        <div style="font-size: 3rem; font-weight: 700;">$150</div>
                        <div style="font-size: 0.95rem;">Regularly $200 • Save $50</div>
                        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; opacity: 0.9; margin-top: 5px;">Mention this special at booking or service to receive promotional pricing</div>
                        <div style="font-size: 0.85rem; opacity: 0.9; margin-top: 5px;">Valid through September 1, 2026</div>
                    </div>

                    <div style="max-width: 760px; margin: 0 auto 30px; font-size: 0.95rem; opacity: 0.95;">
                        Promotional rate applies to standard one-story, ground-level dryer vent access. Roof access, difficult ladder placement, elevated exterior vents, unusually long vent runs, or heavily restricted systems may require a custom quote.
                    </div>

                    <div>
                        <a href="tel:9374780689" class="btn btn-accent btn-lg btn-pulse">
                            <i class="fas fa-phone-alt"></i> Call Now: 937-478-0689
                        </a>
                    </div>
                </div>
            </div>
        </section>

        <section style="padding: 60px 0; background: #fff;">
            <div class="container">
                <div class="warning-box" data-aos="fade-up" style="border-color: #e74c3c; background: #fdf2f2;">
                    <div class="warning-content">
                        <strong style="color: #e74c3c;"><i class="fas fa-fire" style="margin-right: 10px;"></i>Why Dryer Vent Cleaning Matters</strong><br><br>
                        A clogged dryer vent can restrict airflow, cause your dryer to run longer, increase heat buildup, and create a serious fire concern. If your clothes are taking longer to dry, your dryer feels hot, or you notice a burning smell, it is time to have the vent checked.
                        <br><br>
                        <span class="price-highlight" style="color: #e74c3c;">Summer Special: $150, regularly $200. Save $50 when you mention this special.</span>
                    </div>
                </div>
            </div>
        </section>

        <section class="benefits-section" style="padding: 60px 0;">
            <div class="container">
                <div class="section-header text-center" data-aos="fade-up">
                    <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;">Why Clean Your Dryer Vent?</h2>
                    <p>The benefits go beyond fire prevention</p>
                </div>

                <div class="benefits-grid" data-aos="fade-up">
                    <div class="benefit-card">
                        <div class="benefit-icon" style="background: #e74c3c;">
                            <i class="fas fa-fire-extinguisher"></i>
                        </div>
                        <h3 class="benefit-title">Reduce Fire Risk</h3>
                        <p>Lint buildup is highly flammable. Cleaning the vent helps reduce heat buildup and improves dryer safety.</p>
                    </div>

                    <div class="benefit-card">
                        <div class="benefit-icon">
                            <i class="fas fa-bolt"></i>
                        </div>
                        <h3 class="benefit-title">Improve Efficiency</h3>
                        <p>A clogged vent makes your dryer work harder and run longer. A clean vent helps restore better airflow.</p>
                    </div>

                    <div class="benefit-card">
                        <div class="benefit-icon">
                            <i class="fas fa-cog"></i>
                        </div>
                        <h3 class="benefit-title">Help Protect the Dryer</h3>
                        <p>When your dryer overheats due to poor ventilation, it can wear out faster and work harder than necessary.</p>
                    </div>

                    <div class="benefit-card">
                        <div class="benefit-icon">
                            <i class="fas fa-tshirt"></i>
                        </div>
                        <h3 class="benefit-title">Faster Drying</h3>
                        <p>If clothes are taking two or three cycles to dry, restricted airflow may be part of the problem.</p>
                    </div>
                </div>

                        <h3>Clothes Take Longer to Dry</h3>
                        <p>If your dryer needs multiple cycles to dry a normal load, restricted airflow from lint buildup may be the cause.</p>
                    </div>

                    <div class="sign-card">
                        <i class="fas fa-temperature-high" style="color: #e74c3c;"></i>

                    </div>

                    </div>

                        <i class="fas fa-wind" style="color: var(--primary);"></i>

                    </div>

        </div>

        <div class="benefits-grid">
          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="50">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-hand-paper"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Hand Cleaning</h3>
            <p>Leaves, sticks, roof grit, shingle granules, seed pods, mud, and other debris are removed from the gutters by hand. Hand blowers are used where appropriate to help finish the cleanup.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="125">

            <p>We use water to flush every downspout and verify that water moves through the vertical system rather than assuming the opening is clear.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="200">

          </article>

            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-camera"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Proof-of-Work Photos</h3>
            <p>You receive detailed photo documentation showing what was found, what was cleared, and the completed condition of the gutter system.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="350">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-tools"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Complimentary Tune-Ups</h3>
            <p>Within reason, we tap loose gutter spikes back into place and may add a few complimentary hangers where needed to help secure minor problem areas.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="425">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-broom"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Ground Cleanup</h3>
            <p>Removed debris is collected and the work area is cleaned. We do not consider the job complete while gutter debris is scattered around your property.</p>
          </article>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section-pad" style="background:#fff;">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="service-detail" data-aos="fade-up">
          <div
            class="service-detail-image brand-media brand-media--cleaning"
            role="img"
            aria-label="CleanFlow of Ohio gutter cleaning: clear, flush, assess, document"
          >
            <i class="fas fa-broom" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <span>Clear &middot; Flush &middot; Assess &middot; Document</span>
          </div>

          <div class="service-detail-content">
            <div class="service-detail-header">
              <div class="service-icon"><i class="fas fa-clipboard-check"></i></div>
              <div>
                <span class="service-eyebrow">Clear, flush, assess, document</span>
                <h2>A Complete System Check, Not a Quick Scoop-Out</h2>
              </div>
            </div>

            <p class="service-desc">A gutter can look clean from the ground while a downspout remains restricted or an underground line backs up as soon as water reaches it. That is why water testing is part of our normal process.</p>

            <ul class="checkmark-list">
              <li>Gutters cleared by hand</li>
              <li>Every downspout flushed with water</li>
              <li>Visible water flow confirmed at downspout outlets</li>
              <li>Connected underground lines checked when accessible</li>
              <li>Visible leaks, sagging, loose sections, pitch concerns, and worn components noted</li>
              <li>Minor complimentary spike and hanger support when reasonable</li>
              <li>Grounds cleaned and debris removed</li>
              <li>Detailed proof-of-work photos provided</li>
            </ul>

            <div class="pricing-note">
              <i class="fas fa-tag"></i>
              Gutter cleaning starts at <strong>$150</strong> for standard homes. Final pricing depends on access, height, debris level, guards, downspout restrictions, and overall job difficulty.
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section-pad alt-bg">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="section-header text-center" data-aos="fade-up">
          <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;">Signs Your Gutters Need Attention</h2>
          <p>These symptoms can point to debris, a restricted downspout, an underground flow problem, or a condition that needs a closer look.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="signs-grid">
          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="50">
            <i class="fas fa-water"></i>
            <h3>Water Over the Front Edge</h3>
            <p>Overflow during rain often means leaves, roof grit, or compacted debris are restricting the gutter or outlet.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="125">
            <i class="fas fa-arrow-up"></i>
            <h3>Water Backs Up at a Downspout</h3>
            <p>A blockage may be inside the outlet, elbow, vertical downspout, or underground line below it.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="200">
            <i class="fas fa-seedling"></i>
            <h3>Plants or Moss in the Gutters</h3>
            <p>Organic growth usually means moisture and decomposing debris have been sitting in the gutter for an extended period.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="275">
            <i class="fas fa-weight-hanging"></i>
            <h3>Sagging or Pulling Away</h3>
            <p>Wet debris adds weight and can worsen loose spikes, hangers, low areas, and sections already pulling from the fascia.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="350">
            <i class="fas fa-home"></i>
            <h3>Water Near the Foundation</h3>
            <p>The gutters may be clear while a downspout outlet, underground line, or final discharge point is not moving water away properly.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="425">
            <i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i>
            <h3>Guards Still Overflow</h3>
            <p>Guarded systems can collect fine debris, roof grit, and material at valleys or openings. They still need inspection and flow verification.</p>
          </article>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section-pad" style="background:#fff;">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="warning-box" data-aos="fade-right" style="background:#f0f4f8;border-color:var(--primary);">
          <div class="warning-content">
            <strong style="color:var(--primary-dark);"><i class="fas fa-snowflake" style="margin-right:10px;"></i>Fall Cleaning Is Winter Preparation</strong><br><br>
            Going into freezing weather with gutters and downspouts packed with wet leaves, roof grit, and debris can create much larger problems. Trapped water can freeze and expand, stress gutter seams and downspout connections, crack or separate sections, loosen gutters, and add substantial weight to the system.
            <br><br>
            Full gutters can also increase freeze-and-thaw trouble and contribute to ice buildup along the roofline. Late leaves do not always fall on schedule, so some properties benefit from a final winter-prep cleaning after the last major leaf drop.
            <span class="price-highlight" style="color:var(--primary);">The goal is to enter winter with the gutters, downspouts, and connected drainage path clear and moving water.</span>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

            <h3>Complimentary Unclog Support</h3>
            <p>Qualifying clogs between scheduled visits are handled complimentary, typically within 48 hours, subject to weather, safety, access, and plan terms.</p>
          </article>
        </div>

        <div class="text-center mt-3" data-aos="zoom-in">
          <p style="color:white;max-width:820px;margin:0 auto 24px;">Ask how to save up to 15% with a service plan. Easy Pay options may provide additional savings depending on the selected plan and payment arrangement.</p>
          <a href="tel:9374780689" class="btn btn-accent btn-lg"><i class="fas fa-phone-alt"></i> Ask About Service Plans</a>

                        <p style="font-size: 1.2rem; color: var(--gray); margin-bottom: 30px;">Protect your home's foundation and roofline with heavy-duty, custom-fabricated 5-inch and 6-inch seamless aluminum gutters. Installed right the first time by a 20+ year industry veteran and backed by a one-year CleanFlow installation workmanship warranty.</p>
                        <ul class="checkmark-list mb-4" style="font-weight: 500;">

        <section class="section-pad" style="background: #fff;">
            <div class="container">
                <div class="section-header text-center" data-aos="fade-up">
                    <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;">Why Upgrade to Seamless Gutters?</h2>
                    <p>Sectional gutters are a thing of the past. Here is why seamless is the only way to go.</p>
                </div>
                <div class="grid grid-3" data-aos="fade-up">
                    <div class="service-card" style="padding: 30px; text-align: center;">
                        <i class="fas fa-tint-slash" style="font-size: 40px; color: var(--primary); margin-bottom: 20px;"></i>
                        <h3>Fewer Leak Points</h3>
                        <p>With no seams running along the length of each gutter, there are far fewer potential leak points where water can escape and reach your fascia boards.</p>
                    </div>
                    <div class="service-card" style="padding: 30px; text-align: center;">
                        <i class="fas fa-ruler-combined" style="font-size: 40px; color: var(--primary); margin-bottom: 20px;"></i>
                        <h3>Custom On-Site Fit</h3>
                        <p>We roll-form your new gutters right in your driveway, ensuring exact measurements tailored perfectly to your home's unique roofline.</p>
                    </div>
                    <div class="service-card" style="padding: 30px; text-align: center;">
                        <i class="fas fa-shield-alt" style="font-size: 40px; color: var(--primary); margin-bottom: 20px;"></i>
                        <h3>.032 Gauge Durability</h3>
                        <p>We don't use flimsy builder-grade materials. Our .032 gauge aluminum withstands heavy Ohio snow, ice, and severe summer storms.</p>
                    </div>
                </div>
            </div>
        </section>

        <section class="section-pad" style="background: var(--primary-dark); color: white;">

                        <h2 style="color: white;">5-Inch vs. 6-Inch Gutters:<br>What Do You Need?</h2>
                        <p style="color: rgba(255,255,255,0.8); margin-bottom: 20px;">One of the most common questions I get asked. Sizing your system properly is the difference between a dry basement and an overflowing mess during a heavy downpour.</p>
                        <div style="background: rgba(255,255,255,0.1); padding: 20px; border-radius: 10px; margin-bottom: 15px;">
                            <h3 style="color: var(--accent); margin-bottom: 10px; font-size: 1.15rem;">5-Inch Seamless Gutters</h3>
                            <p style="margin: 0; font-size: 0.95rem;">The industry standard for most traditional residential homes in the Miami Valley area. Perfect for standard pitched roofs and average rainfall.</p>
                        </div>
                        <div style="background: rgba(255,255,255,0.1); padding: 20px; border-radius: 10px;">
                            <h3 style="color: var(--accent); margin-bottom: 10px; font-size: 1.15rem;">6-Inch Seamless Gutters</h3>
                            <p style="margin: 0; font-size: 0.95rem;">Greater capacity for larger roof areas and heavier water flow. Highly recommended for large or steep roofs, metal roofs, or homes that regularly experience heavy runoff pooling near the foundation.</p>
                        </div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="text-center">
                        <i class="fas fa-home" style="font-size: 150px; color: rgba(255,255,255,0.1);"></i>
                    </div>
                </div>
            </div>
        </section>

          <div class="hero-kicker">CleanFlow of Ohio Drainage</div>
          <h1>Underground Downspout &amp; Yard Drainage Solutions in Dayton, Ohio</h1>
          <p>Buried downspout lines that back up, water collecting against the foundation, and yards that stay soggy long after the rain stops. We start by working out where the water begins, where it stops moving, and where it can safely go &mdash; then recommend the least invasive fix that actually addresses the cause. Serving Dayton and the greater Miami Valley.</p>

          <div class="service-hero-badges">
            <span><i class="fas fa-search" aria-hidden="true"></i> Diagnosis First</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-route" aria-hidden="true"></i> Solid PVC Conveyance</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-tools" aria-hidden="true"></i> Cleanout Access Built In</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-shield-alt" aria-hidden="true"></i> Fully insured and bonded</span>
          </div>

          <div class="services-hero-actions">
            <a href="tel:9374780689" class="btn hero-main-cta"><i class="fas fa-phone-alt"></i> Call 937-478-0689</a>
            <a href="/#quote" class="btn hero-call-cta"><i class="fas fa-clipboard-check"></i> Request a Drainage Assessment</a>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section-pad alt-bg">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="section-header text-center" data-aos="fade-up">
          <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;">What Homeowners Usually Notice First</h2>
          <p>Drainage problems rarely announce themselves as drainage problems. These are the symptoms that bring most people to this page.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="signs-grid">
          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="50">
            <i class="fas fa-arrow-up" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>The Buried Downspout Backs Up</h3>
            <p>Water surfaces at the connection during rain instead of disappearing into the ground. The line is accepting less than the roof is sending it, or nothing at all.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="100">
            <i class="fas fa-tint" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>Water Spills at the Connection</h3>
            <p>The downspout and the buried pipe have separated, cracked, or filled in, so water escapes right where the two meet.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="150">
            <i class="fas fa-home" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>Water Pooling Beside the Foundation</h3>
            <p>Roof runoff is being released too close to the house, or the ground beside it no longer moves water away.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="200">
            <i class="fas fa-seedling" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>A Soggy, Unusable Part of the Yard</h3>
            <p>An area stays saturated for days. It may be receiving roof water, catching runoff from higher ground, or sitting where water has nowhere to go.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="250">
            <i class="fas fa-warehouse" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>Runoff Heading the Wrong Direction</h3>
            <p>Water tracks toward a garage, patio, walkway, or door instead of away from the structures you use.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="300">
            <i class="fas fa-clock" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>A Drain That Takes Water Slowly</h3>
            <p>It works, but not at the rate a real downpour demands. Partial restriction is common and easy to miss until a heavy storm.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="350">
            <i class="fas fa-question-circle" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>Nobody Knows Where the Line Goes</h3>
            <p>A pipe enters the ground and no one can say where it comes out, whether it still runs anywhere, or if it was ever connected to an outlet.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="sign-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="400">
            <i class="fas fa-arrows-alt-h" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>Sump Discharge Too Close to the House</h3>
            <p>The pump is doing its job, then releasing the water a few feet from the foundation where it can work its way back down.</p>
          </article>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section-pad" style="background:#fff;">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="service-detail" data-aos="fade-up">
          <div
            class="service-detail-image brand-media brand-media--drainage"
            role="img"
            aria-label="CleanFlow of Ohio drainage approach: source, path, restriction, outlet"
          >
            <i class="fas fa-water" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <span>Source &middot; Path &middot; Restriction &middot; Outlet</span>
          </div>

          <div class="service-detail-content">
            <div class="service-detail-header">
              <div class="service-icon"><i class="fas fa-search" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
              <div>
                <span class="service-eyebrow">Diagnosis before digging</span>
                <h2>The Right Fix Depends on Where the Water Actually Stops</h2>
              </div>
            </div>

            <p class="service-desc">Two properties can show the same puddle for entirely different reasons. One has a downspout line packed with silt; the next has a sound line discharging to a spot that no longer drains. Guessing costs money and often moves the problem rather than solving it, so we work the system in order.</p>

            <ul class="checkmark-list">
              <li>Identify the water source &mdash; roof runoff, surface runoff, a sump discharge, or ground water moving beneath the surface</li>
              <li>Inspect and test the existing path with water wherever it is accessible</li>
              <li>Determine the likely restriction, failure, or simply an outlet that cannot keep up</li>
              <li>Evaluate the grade and identify realistic discharge locations for the property</li>
              <li>Recommend the least invasive practical solution that addresses the cause</li>
              <li>Explain plainly when a repair is enough, when replacement makes more sense, and when a different method belongs in the plan</li>
            </ul>

            <p class="service-desc">The correct solution depends on the source of the water, the existing grade, the condition of the current system, and the safest approved discharge point. That is a property-by-property answer, not a package.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="service-card-showcase-section">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="section-header text-center" data-aos="fade-up">
          <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;">Drainage Services and Solutions</h2>
          <p>These are the tools we draw from. A drainage plan uses the ones the property needs &mdash; no property gets the whole list.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="benefits-grid">
          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="50">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-vial" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Existing Line Testing &amp; Unclogging</h3>
            <p>We run water into the existing buried line and watch what it does. Where a line is accessible and sound enough to work with, jetting can clear silt, sediment, and root intrusion. Not every buried line can be cleared this way, and we will tell you when we hit that limit rather than keep charging at it.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="100">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-wrench" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Underground Downspout Repair &amp; Replacement</h3>
            <p>Crushed sections, separated joints, collapsed corrugated pipe, and lines that have filled in past recovery. Sometimes a short section is the whole problem; sometimes the run has reached the end of its service life and replacing it costs less than chasing it.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="150">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-route" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">New Solid PVC Downspout Drainage</h3>
            <p>New underground downspout conveyance built with solid PVC, gradual fittings, and cleanout access, carrying roof water away from the foundation to a discharge point the property can actually support.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="200">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-grip-lines" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Catch Basins &amp; Surface Drains</h3>
            <p>Where surface water collects in a defined low area, a catch basin gives it a place to enter the system and a sediment sump that can be cleaned out later instead of silting the whole run.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="250">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-road" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Channel Drains</h3>
            <p>Suited to hard surfaces &mdash; a driveway apron, garage entry, patio edge, or walkway &mdash; where water runs as a sheet across pavement and needs intercepting along a line rather than at a single point.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="300">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-layer-group" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">French Drains, Where They Fit</h3>
            <p>A French drain collects water moving through the soil. That makes it the right answer for subsurface and ground water problems and the wrong answer for a clogged downspout line. We use them where the water is actually in the ground, not as a default.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="350">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-mountain" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Grading &amp; Water Channeling</h3>
            <p>Sometimes the most durable fix is shaping the ground so water leaves on its own. Practical regrading and channeling can reduce how much has to be piped in the first place.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="400">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-pump-soap" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Dedicated Sump Discharge</h3>
            <p>A sump pump needs its own route to its own outlet, sized and placed so the water it removes does not simply return. This is always planned as a separate line.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="450">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-leaf" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Pop-Up Emitters &amp; Dry Wells</h3>
            <p>A pop-up emitter releases water at a chosen point away from the home and closes back down between rains. A dry well holds volume and lets it soak away &mdash; useful where soil and site conditions allow it, and unsuitable where they do not.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="500">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-hard-hat" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Sidewalk Boring &amp; Concrete Access</h3>
            <p>Where a line has to cross a sidewalk or slab, boring underneath usually avoids cutting it. When concrete access genuinely cannot be avoided, we say so before the work starts and handle the excavation and restoration.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="550">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-map-signs" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Approved Discharge Connections</h3>
            <p>Some properties have a roadside ditch, curb, catch basin, or municipal outlet available. Those connections are possible where an approved outlet exists and when permitted &mdash; which is a question we settle before promising a route, not after.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="benefit-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="600">
            <div class="benefit-icon"><i class="fas fa-seedling" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
            <h3 class="benefit-title">Backfill &amp; Landscape Restoration</h3>
            <p>Turf and plantings are protected where practical, trenches are backfilled and compacted, and the work area is restored to a reasonable condition rather than left as a scar across the yard.</p>
          </article>
        </div>

        <div class="warning-box" data-aos="fade-right" style="background:#f0f4f8;border-color:var(--primary);">
          <div class="warning-content">
            <strong style="color:var(--primary-dark);"><i class="fas fa-pump-soap" style="margin-right:10px;" aria-hidden="true"></i>Sump Discharge Is Always Its Own Route</strong><br><br>
            A sump pump can move a large volume of water in a short burst, and it runs on its own schedule rather than the weather's. Tying that discharge into an existing underground downspout line means the two compete for the same pipe at the worst possible moment &mdash; and a restriction anywhere in that shared run sends water back toward the house.
            <br><br>
            CleanFlow evaluates sump discharge as a separate, dedicated route with its own outlet.
            <span class="price-highlight" style="color:var(--primary);">We do not recommend connecting a sump-pump discharge into an existing underground downspout line.</span>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section-pad alt-bg">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="service-detail reverse" data-aos="fade-up">
          <div
            class="service-detail-image brand-media brand-media--drainage"
            role="img"
            aria-label="CleanFlow of Ohio drainage construction standards: solid PVC, gradual fittings, cleanout access"
          >
            <i class="fas fa-tools" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <span>Built for Flow &middot; Built for Access</span>
          </div>

          <div class="service-detail-content">
            <div class="service-detail-header">
              <div class="service-icon"><i class="fas fa-hard-hat" aria-hidden="true"></i></div>
              <div>
                <span class="service-eyebrow">How we build it</span>
                <h2>Built for Flow and Future Access</h2>
              </div>
            </div>

            <p class="service-desc">Most of the failed underground downspout lines we dig up were not badly damaged. They were built in a way that made them impossible to maintain and easy to block. Where site conditions and project scope allow, this is how CleanFlow builds instead.</p>

            <ul class="checkmark-list">
              <li><strong>ASTM 2729 solid PVC</strong> for underground downspout conveyance &mdash; smooth wall, so silt and debris keep moving instead of settling into ridges</li>
              <li><strong>No corrugated pipe</strong> on new solid downspout-conveyance runs. Corrugation traps sediment, crushes under load, and is the most common thing we replace</li>
              <li><strong>Gradual 45-degree fittings underground</strong> rather than sharp 90-degree turns, so debris has a path through the bend instead of a wall to pack against</li>
              <li><strong>Wye cleanouts with removable plugs</strong> at downspout transitions, so the line can be opened and cleared later without excavation</li>
              <li><strong>Roughly 1 to 2 percent slope</strong> where site conditions permit &mdash; enough fall to keep solids moving with the water</li>
              <li><strong>Accessible maintenance points</strong> placed where they can practically be reached, not buried and forgotten</li>
              <li><strong>A discharge point chosen for the property</strong> and an approved outlet, rather than the nearest convenient spot</li>
              <li><strong>Landscape protection, proper backfill, and reasonable restoration</strong> as part of the job rather than an afterthought</li>
              <li><strong>Follow-up consideration for normal soil settling</strong> where that is included in the project scope</li>
            </ul>

            <p class="service-desc">Depth, slope, and outlet are decided by the property. Utility locations, existing structures, frost considerations, tree roots, and where the water can legally and practically go all shape the final design, so we do not publish a single number and apply it everywhere.</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>

    <section class="section-pad" style="background:var(--primary-dark);color:white;">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="section-header text-center" data-aos="fade-up">
          <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;color:white;">What to Expect</h2>
          <p style="color:rgba(255,255,255,0.88);">Drainage projects vary widely in scope, so the timeline does too. The sequence does not.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="grid grid-3">
          <article class="service-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="50" style="padding:30px;">
            <i class="fas fa-search" style="font-size:40px;color:var(--accent);margin-bottom:20px;" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>1. Assessment</h3>
            <p>We walk the property, look at the roof and the ground together, test what is accessible with water, and find out what happens during real rain.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="service-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="125" style="padding:30px;">
            <i class="fas fa-comments" style="font-size:40px;color:var(--accent);margin-bottom:20px;" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>2. Findings &amp; Proposed Solution</h3>
            <p>You hear what we found, what we think is causing it, and which approach we recommend &mdash; including the options we considered and set aside, and why.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="service-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="200" style="padding:30px;">
            <i class="fas fa-file-signature" style="font-size:40px;color:var(--accent);margin-bottom:20px;" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>3. Clear Written Estimate</h3>
            <p>Scope, materials, and price in writing before anything is dug. Where approvals, permits, or utility locating apply, that is identified up front.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="service-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="275" style="padding:30px;">
            <i class="fas fa-hard-hat" style="font-size:40px;color:var(--accent);margin-bottom:20px;" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>4. Installation or Repair</h3>
            <p>The work itself, built to the standards above, with landscaping protected where practical and the site kept as contained as the job allows.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="service-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="350" style="padding:30px;">
            <i class="fas fa-water" style="font-size:40px;color:var(--accent);margin-bottom:20px;" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>5. Flow Verification</h3>
            <p>Water goes through the finished system while we watch it. A drainage line is not finished because it is buried; it is finished because it moves water.</p>
          </article>

          <article class="service-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="425" style="padding:30px;">
            <i class="fas fa-camera" style="font-size:40px;color:var(--accent);margin-bottom:20px;" aria-hidden="true"></i>
            <h3>6. Cleanup &amp; Documentation</h3>
            <p>Backfill, restoration, and photos of what was found and what was built &mdash; including where the cleanouts are, so the next person is not guessing.</p>
          </article>
        </div>

        <div class="text-center mt-3" data-aos="zoom-in">
          <p style="color:white;max-width:820px;margin:0 auto 24px;">Drainage pricing is property-specific. Trench length, depth, surface type, access, restoration, and the available outlet all change the number, so we price the project in front of us rather than publishing a rate that would not apply to your home.</p>
          <a href="tel:9374780689" class="btn btn-accent btn-lg"><i class="fas fa-phone-alt"></i> Talk Through Your Drainage Problem</a>

          <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;">Real Drainage Work, in Customers&rsquo; Words</h2>
          <p>Two Google reviews from drainage and downspout customers in the Miami Valley.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="grid grid-2">
          <figure class="review-card" data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-delay="50">

    <section class="section-pad alt-bg">
      <div class="container">
        <div class="section-header text-center" data-aos="fade-up">
          <h2 style="margin-left:auto;margin-right:auto;">Drainage Questions We Get Asked</h2>
          <p>Straight answers about buried downspout lines, method selection, and what happens to your yard.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="accordion" data-aos="fade-up">
          <div class="accordion-item">
            <h3 class="accordion-heading">
              <button
                type="button"
                class="accordion-header"
                onclick="toggleAccordion(this)"
                aria-expanded="false"
                aria-controls="drainage-faq-1"
              >
                <span>Why does my underground downspout back up?</span>
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down" aria-hidden="true"></i>
              </button>
            </h3>
            <div class="accordion-content" id="drainage-faq-1" role="region">
              <p>Usually one of four things. The line has filled with silt, roof grit, and shingle granules that washed down over the years. Roots have found a joint and grown into it. A section has crushed, separated, or collapsed &mdash; common with older corrugated pipe. Or the pipe is sound but the outlet is buried, blocked, or was never adequate for the volume the roof delivers. Testing with water tells us which one it is, and the answer changes the fix completely.</p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="accordion-item">
            <h3 class="accordion-heading">
              <button
                type="button"
                class="accordion-header"
                onclick="toggleAccordion(this)"
                aria-expanded="false"
                aria-controls="drainage-faq-2"
              >
                <span>Can my existing buried line be unclogged, or does it need replacing?</span>
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down" aria-hidden="true"></i>
              </button>
            </h3>
            <div class="accordion-content" id="drainage-faq-2" role="region">
              <p>It depends on what the line is made of, what condition it is in, and whether we can reach it. Accessible lines that are structurally sound can often be jetted clear of silt and roots. Lines that are crushed, separated, collapsed, or so far gone that clearing them would not last are better replaced. We do not claim every buried line can be cleared &mdash; some cannot, and jetting a failed line is money spent twice. You will get an honest read on which situation you are in before any work is agreed.</p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="accordion-item">
            <h3 class="accordion-heading">
              <button
                type="button"
                class="accordion-header"
                onclick="toggleAccordion(this)"
                aria-expanded="false"
                aria-controls="drainage-faq-3"
              >
                <span>What pipe do you use for new underground downspout drainage?</span>
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down" aria-hidden="true"></i>
              </button>
            </h3>
            <div class="accordion-content" id="drainage-faq-3" role="region">
              <p>ASTM 2729 solid PVC for downspout conveyance, with gradual 45-degree fittings instead of sharp underground 90-degree turns, and wye cleanouts with removable plugs at the downspout transitions. We do not use corrugated pipe for new solid downspout-conveyance runs. The smooth wall keeps sediment moving rather than letting it settle, the gentler bends give debris a way through, and the cleanouts mean the line can be opened and cleared years later without digging up the yard.</p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="accordion-item">
            <h3 class="accordion-heading">
              <button
                type="button"
                class="accordion-header"
                onclick="toggleAccordion(this)"
                aria-expanded="false"
                aria-controls="drainage-faq-4"
              >
                <span>Is a French drain always the right answer?</span>
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down" aria-hidden="true"></i>
              </button>
            </h3>
            <div class="accordion-content" id="drainage-faq-4" role="region">
              <p>No. A French drain is built to collect water moving through the soil, which makes it a strong solution for subsurface and ground water and a poor one for a blocked downspout line. Installing a French drain when the real problem is a clogged buried pipe adds cost without addressing the cause. It is one method among several &mdash; alongside solid PVC conveyance, catch basins, channel drains, grading, pop-up emitters, and dry wells &mdash; and it earns its place only when the water is genuinely in the ground.</p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="accordion-item">
            <h3 class="accordion-heading">
              <button
                type="button"
                class="accordion-header"
                onclick="toggleAccordion(this)"
                aria-expanded="false"
                aria-controls="drainage-faq-5"
              >
                <span>Where can the water actually discharge?</span>
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down" aria-hidden="true"></i>
              </button>
            </h3>
            <div class="accordion-content" id="drainage-faq-5" role="region">
              <p>That is decided by the property, not by preference. Options can include a lower point on the lot, a pop-up emitter, a dry well where soil and site conditions allow, or a connection to a roadside ditch, curb, catch basin, or public drainage outlet where an approved outlet is available and when permitted. Some of those require property-specific approval, utility locating, right-of-way permission, municipal approval, or a permit or bond. CleanFlow does not have automatic permission to connect to a road, curb, catch basin, storm sewer, or municipal system, so the available outlet is something we establish during the assessment &mdash; subject to property conditions and local requirements.</p>
            </div>
          </div>

          <div class="accordion-item">
            <h3 class="accordion-heading">
              <button
                type="button"
                class="accordion-header"
                onclick="toggleAccordion(this)"
                aria-expanded="false"
                aria-controls="drainage-faq-6"
              >
                <span>What happens to my landscaping and the areas you dig?</span>
                <i class="fas fa-chevron-down" aria-hidden="true"></i>
              </button>
            </h3>
            <div class="accordion-content" id="drainage-faq-6" role="region">
              <p>Turf and plantings are protected where practical, and we plan the route to work around what matters to you when the site allows it. Trenches are backfilled and compacted, and the work area is restored to a reasonable condition. Some settling over the following months is normal as backfilled soil consolidates, and where it is part of the project scope we account for follow-up on that. Where a sidewalk or slab is in the way, boring underneath usually avoids cutting it; if concrete access genuinely cannot be avoided, you will hear that before the work starts, not after.</p>
            </div>
          </div>
        </div>
      </div>
    </section>
